children: Consumers' expectations for future inflation in August were unchanged at short and longer-term horizons, according to a New York Fed survey.

Consumers' expectations for future inflation at the one-year and five-year-ahead horizons were unchanged at 3.6% and 3.0%, according to the latest monthly version of the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations. At the three-year horizon they decreased slightly to 3.2%.

If consumers anticipate higher prices in the future, they may accelerate purchases, ask for larger raises, and worsen their overall sentiment toward any economic progress. Tuesday's inflation expectations figures should serve as a welcome signal for the central bank who focus on making sure consumer expectations don't become self-fulfilling.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at his debut Jackson Hole speech last month that measures of inflation expectations in the medium term, by and large, look stable.

"The thing about market measures of inflation expectations in economic history is that they tend to look strong and durable until they don't," Warsh said last month. "It's the Fed's job to make sure that inflation expectations do not get unanchored."

As August's employment report came in better than analysts were expecting, market participants and Fed officials will focus their attention on the consumer price index print this Friday ahead of the Fed's interest rate decision on Sept. 16.

Consumer inflation has risen in large part due to higher gasoline prices tied to the Iran conflict. The NY Fed survey found that median year-ahead expected price changes increased by 1.7 percentage points to 4.6% for gasoline.

The survey also found that labor market expectations were mixed. The mean probability that the U.S. unemployment rate will be higher one year from now-increased by 1.6 percentage points to 44.4%, its highest reading since April 2020.
However, the mean perceived probability of losing one's job in the next year fell to its lowest reading since February 2026.
